paragraphs.text: Nath was a taercenn of the Gilt-Leaf hunters. As supreme huntmaster , Nath was one of the most seasoned warriors of the Gilt-Leaf tribe and despised everything that was considered ugly by elvish standards. Nath was a ruthless commander, knowing no mercy and never hesitating to kill any of his subordinates when they failed.

By 4520 AR , Nath was already an old and wizened creature, and he hid his true appearance behind a glamer spell. This glamer failed only under the most strained conditions, such as when Nath was unconscious, but was not easily dispelled in battle; indeed, Nath maintained his position by appearing to all as an imposing elf armored in rare silverwood bark and a magnificent crown of horns. Nath carried an imposing authority about him that made him seem capable of ordering the death of any creature with just a single word.

Nath arrived to punish Daen Rhys of the Hemlock pack upon discovering that the daen had hired two giants — regularly considered repulsive eyeblights by the elves— as a backup plan for pacifying a boggart settlement within their territory. Nath considered the raid a devastating, inelegant failure. He plunged his sword into the still-living skull of Yelm , a young hunter who had caused the attack to derail when he loosed an arrow prematurely. He demoted Rhys and gave the command of the Hemlock pack to Rhys' second-in-command, Daen Gryffid .

Later, Nath ordered the full strength of the Gilt-Leaf hunters to attack boggarts converging in the Porringer Valley . Rhys was reluctant and tried to convince Nath to call off the attack after he recognized the gathering as the peaceful Feast of Footbottom ; they would be slaying innocents and in doing so would also risk jeopardizing their tenuous standing with the valley's treefolk . Nath was disgusted and exasperated by his subordinate's compassion for these lesser races and revealed that he aimed to ambush their disgusting festival to eradicate them with greater ease. In their success, Nath hoped to create a new Gilt-Leaf outpost.

The organized hunters at first suffered no retaliation, with scores of boggarts being killed and burned alive before they even realized they were in danger. Nath drew the power of the woods to rally his forces, and Rhys used his magic to turn the forest floor into razor-sharp arrowgrass for which to nock their bows. Their incursion went awry when the boggarts suddenly became enraged and started to fight back as feral, wild animals. The elves now found themselves overwhelmed, and Nath ordered them all to fight to their last breath. In desperation and spurred on by Gryffid, Rhys called for the might of his yew poison magic to turn the tables from crushing defeat. The resulting blast defiled a huge portion of the forest and wiped out the combatants, with the only three confirmed survivors: Rhys, of course, withstood his own wayward spell, Gryffid survived by virtue of being in proximity to the blast's point of origin, and Nath was shielded by the corpse of his cervin mount, which was cut down earlier amidst the bloodshed. Rhys lost his horns and fled, and Nath's appearance-altering glamer had faded. Gryffid saw Nath in his hideous true form and was offered the following: either keep Nath's secret and be properly rewarded, or betray him and be transformed into a vinebred soldier. After Gryffid chose to ally himself, Nath healed him and promoted him to the exquisite class.

Nath now had to carefully balance the futures of the two elves who could ruin his reputation: Gryffid, who now knew the secret of his disfigurement, and Rhys, the only other survivor of the incident who could expose Nath's poor judgment in authorizing the ill-fated attack that cost the lives of the assembled hunting packs. For the latter, Nath sought immediate death.

During the Festival of Tales , Nath and Gryffid came to Kinsbaile in pursuit of Rhys; Nath's personal distaste of Rhys and his morals had by now boiled over into a personal vendetta and saw it as his duty to bring him to justice. The taercenn planned to use the opportunity to annex Kinsbaile and build an elvish outpost there, and the incompetent local leader Gaddock Teeg fell to order immediately. There, they set out to ambush Rhys. Nath was angered by the need to lower himself to keeping the company of the kithkin, and bided his time daydreaming about different gruesome scenarios of eradicating them as he impatiently lay in wait for the disgraced hunter.

When Rhys returned, Nath challenged him to a duel to provide him a hunter's death and tossed a silver blade at his feet. Surrounded by vinebred warriors and an army of assembled elves who would not hesitate to kill him if he managed to gain any upper hand over Nath in battle, Rhys strategically fled into the woods, determined to meet the taercenn elsewhere and on different terms. Nath rode out on a new sunrise yellow cervin to give chase, and his cuffhounds badly wounded Rhys and stopped him from fleeing any further. The hounds stopped just short of mauling him to death as Nath called them off so he could finish him off personally, declaring that he would die disgraced and wallowing in his own blood. The battle then devolved into a bloody hand-to-hand brawl, and Rhys emerged victorious when he gripped Nath's horns and twisted them with such might until he snapped his neck and broke off one of his horns. Nath gave out one final scream, which was echoed by the few Gilt-Leaf hunters that managed to catch up to them. Upon the taercenn's death, his glamer spell failed, and his hunting party saw him, finally, as the wretched figure that he concealed from the empire.

His wrinkled form was later found by Gryffid and other hunters. Gryffid set up a funeral pyre for Nath, took his silver sword, and swore a revenge vow — that he would find Rhys and kill him for this, shall woe betide a half of Lorwyn during his hunt or not.

Rhys, victorious on the field of battle, raised the taercenn's broken horn for his detachment of hunters to see. He declared that no word of Nath's true, weathered, and hardened appearance needed to reach the Blessed Nation and told them that if they valued his memory, to honor it.

In the forty years since his death, the grove where Nath was interred had gone wild, becoming host to all manner of deadly, poisonous plants, and legends said that Nath's soul still yearned for revenge.
